title: Why rounding fails
summary: Why the simplex answer is not always a plan: whole numbers only, the optimum as an upper bound, the whole-number points either side of it, and the best practical plan. A graph beside the working shows the region, its whole-number points and the profit line.

els.text: Whole numbers and the simplex answer

slides.title: The simplex answer
slides.brief: The one worked problem for the whole deck. Whole numbers only: the optimum is a corner with fractions in it.

els.text: A stall makes tables ($x$) and chairs ($y$)

els.latex: \begin{array}{l}\text{Maximise } P = 3x + 4y\\[2ex] x + y \le 6\\[1ex] x + 3y \le 11\\[1ex] x \ge 0,\; y \ge 0\end{array}

els.text: We cannot make $3\tfrac{1}{2}$ tables. Only whole numbers of each can be made.
Explain why the simplex answer may not be a plan, and find the best whole-number one.

•  See why rounding to the nearest is not safe
•  Use the simplex answer as an upper bound
•  Test the whole-number points around it and pick the best

slides.title: Can we just round?
slides.brief: 7/2 rounds to 4 and 5/2 rounds to 3 (halves round up). (4, 3) is outside the region: 7 > 6 and 13 > 11.

els.text: Round to the nearest whole number
Is it allowed? Test both limits.
It breaks both limits. Rounding to the nearest is not safe.

slides.title: An upper bound
slides.brief: The orange line is P = 41/2, through the optimum. A whole-number plan is inside the region, so it cannot be above that line; its P is a whole number, so at most 20.

els.text: No whole-number plan can beat the simplex answer
A whole-number plan is also a plan for the linear programme, so its $P$ cannot be more than the simplex's.
The coefficients are whole numbers, so $P$ is a whole number for a whole-number plan.

slides.title: The whole-number points
slides.brief: The lattice points of the region are drawn from the same check the script asserts.

els.text: Only these are plans we can make
Each dot is a whole-number point inside the region.
Green are inside the region. Red are not.

slides.title: Test the four points
slides.brief: (3, 3) breaks only the second limit; (4, 3) breaks both.

els.text: A point is a plan only if it satisfies every limit
$(4, 3)$ is what rounding to the nearest gives. It breaks both limits.
Rounding to the nearest is not safe: test every point.

slides.title: The best practical plan
slides.brief: The region with P above 20 is the thin sliver by the optimum, and it holds no whole-number point: (4, 2), with P = 20, is the best. The green line is P = 20.

els.text: Nothing above $P = 20$ is a whole-number point

els.latex: \begin{array}{l}P = \tfrac{41}{2} \text{ at the optimum}\\[1.2ex]P \le 20 \text{ for a whole-number plan}\end{array}

els.text: $(4, 2)$ has $P = 20$. It reaches the bound, so no practical plan can do better.
The orange sliver is every point with $P > 20$. It holds no whole-number point.
Rounding down gives $(3, 2)$, $P = 17$: practical, but not the best.

•  Is the simplex answer a whole number? If not, it is not a plan.
•  Its $P$ is an upper bound: a whole-number plan has $P$ at most the whole number just below it.
•  Test the whole-number points either side of the optimum: round each variable down and up. A point is a plan only if it satisfies every limit.
•  The best of them is the best plan. If it reaches the bound, no practical plan can do better.

•  Rounding to the nearest can break a limit: always test it.
•  Rounding down is always practical, but it is not always the best plan.
•  Test every limit, not just one: $(3, 3)$ passes one and fails the other.
•  The bound is the whole number just below the optimum's $P$: $20\tfrac{1}{2}$ gives 20, not 21.
